Page structure drawn in depth

Six ideas from the element catalogue, built. Each canvas draws structural elements (<section>, <nav>, <hr>, <header>, <details>, <aside>) in a position the page layout doesn't have: on the faces of a cube, along a curve, at different depths, folded, pulled out towards the reader, and hanging from a string. The elements stay in the document, and the buttons, links and checkboxes inside them are pressed where they are drawn. Drag the cube and the ribbon sideways, and scroll inside the two framed pages.

Navigation on a ribbon

A <nav> with eight links to pages of this site, drawn along a moving curve. Drag sideways to pull the ribbon through. Tap a link to follow it, or long-press it for the browser's link menu.

Each link is drawn in strips 4 px wide, and each strip is turned to the angle of the curve at its place. The link's hit region is its whole box, turned to the angle at its middle.

Slices between hr elements

One <article> with three <hr> elements. The paint handler reads where each <hr> is, cuts the article's picture there, and draws the four slices at different depths. Drag sideways to look from another side.

Header that folds away

Scroll inside the frame. The <header> folds up as the article moves down, and unfolds as soon as the scroll turns back, wherever the reader is in the article.

Field notes

0 marked

Monday. The header above is 96 px tall. It is one element with a heading and a nav, and the canvas draws it over the article.

Scrolling down by 96 px folds it shut. The fold is four strips of the header's picture, each one squashed and leaned to one side, with a shade over it.

Tuesday. The article is taller than the canvas. The canvas does not scroll. It sits in a scroller with an empty block under it, and it draws the article at minus the scroll position.

That keeps the browser's own scrolling: a finger, a wheel, the keyboard and the scroll bar.

Wednesday. Scroll up by any amount and the header starts to unfold, by the same distance.

If the scroll stops while it is half open, it finishes opening or closing by itself.

Thursday. While the header is folded its buttons take no input. When it is flat again it is one plain draw, and Back to top works.

Friday. This is the end of the article.

The scroller is ordinary HTML outside the canvas. A touch that starts on a drawn element scrolls it, because the canvas and everything drawn in it are inside the scroller.

Aside as a margin note on a string

Scroll inside the frame. Each <aside> hangs from a pin beside the paragraph it follows in the markup. A change in scroll speed swings it and stretches its string. Press a note to push it.

A canal lock raises a boat by filling a chamber with water from the higher side. Nothing is pumped.

Pound lockThe kind with two gates.

The gates meet at an angle that points upstream, so the weight of the water holds them shut.

A paddle in each gate lets water through. The crew winds it open with a handle called a windlass.

WindlassEasy to drop in the canal.

When the levels are equal the gate opens with a push on its long beam.

A flight is a run of locks close together. The longest in Britain has 30.

Tardebigge30 locks in about two miles.

Going down, the order is reversed: the chamber is emptied into the lower side.

Each use of a lock moves one chamber of water downhill, so summits need reservoirs.

This is the last paragraph.

The aside is drawn turned about its pin with one drawElementImage() call under a rotation, so its hit region turns with it and the checkbox can be pressed while it swings.

How it works

Each canvas holds the real elements as descendants marked drawable. A paint handler draws them with drawElementImage() under a transform, or in clipped pieces under several transforms. The call also moves the element's hit region to where it was drawn. Four techniques are used more than once:

  • Strips. A 2D context has affine transforms only. Perspective (the cube, the inside of a drawer), a fold (the header) and a bend (the ribbon) are made by drawing the same element many times, each time clipped to a narrow strip with its own transform.
  • One region, several pieces. An element has one hit region, at the place of its last draw. The article in slices and the open drawer are shown in pieces that no single transform covers. A pointerdown listener on the canvas, in the capture phase, finds the piece under the pointer and makes one draw of the element there with globalAlpha = 0. That draw is allowed outside a paint event and moves the region before the browser picks the target of the tap.
  • A canvas inside a scroller. The folding header and the margin notes need a scroll position. The canvas is position: sticky in an ordinary scroller with a spacer under it, and draws the content at minus scrollTop. The browser scrolls it by touch, wheel and keyboard.
  • The element is the state. The cabinet reads open on each paint and the notes read the scroll position. A closed <details> has no picture of its body, so the cabinet keeps a captureElementImage() snapshot of each open drawer and closes the old snapshot when it takes a new one.

Live checks

The checks wait for a tap. Each one builds its own small canvas in a corner of the window, and none of them touches the demos above.

Findings

Measured in headless Chromium 157 on 2026-11-21, at 412 px wide with emulated touch, and at 1000 px wide with a mouse and a keyboard.

  • An element has one hit region, and a canvas can move it before a tap is resolved. A call to drawElementImage() with globalAlpha = 0 made in a pointerdown listener, outside any paint event, moved the region. A touch tap sent with no delay between touch start and touch end then pressed the button in the piece under the finger: in the slices (button, checkbox) and in the drawer body (checkbox, range input, button).
  • The same draw needs an attribute toggle after it. elementFromPoint() at the same point still returned the old answer until an attribute on the element changed. The check "A draw with globalAlpha 0 outside a paint event" shows both answers.
  • Two other routes for the same job were tried on a test page. updateElementGeometry() in the pointerdown listener also worked. Asking for a paint and moving the region in the next paint event was too late for a tap with no delay (the click went to the canvas) and worked for a tap held for 60 ms.
  • A canvas that is position: sticky in a scroller is scrolled natively from its drawn content. A touch drag that started on a drawn paragraph scrolled the scroller, a wheel did too, and the page didn't move. A scroll raises no paint event, so the page asks for one in its scroll listener. An element taller than the canvas, inside the canvas, didn't add to the scroll length.
  • Landmarks and headings stay in the accessibility tree. Chromium's tree (read over the DevTools protocol) lists four regions named Overview, Plan, Sizes and Contact with their headings, the three <nav> elements as navigation landmarks, and all eight ribbon links, including the faces that are turned away and the links that are outside the canvas.
  • Focus can drive the drawing. Tab from the first face moved focus into the second section, which was parked, and the focusin listener turned the cube to it.
  • A link drawn in turned strips is still a link. Its one hit region is its box turned to the angle of the curve. A click on it navigated. A drag of more than 8 px pulled the ribbon and didn't navigate.
  • offsetTop of an <hr> inside a positioned drawable article gives the cut. A clipped draw of the article shows the rows between two cuts and nothing else.
  • A horizontal drag on a canvas with touch-action: pan-y reaches the page, and a vertical one scrolls it. The drag turned the cube by two faces with no page scroll. A vertical swipe on the same face scrolled the page by the length of the swipe.
  • The open drawer hides the drawer below it. Its front is drawn over the next slot and takes the taps there. That matches the picture, and it means the hidden drawer can't be opened until the open one is closed or another visible one is tapped.
  • Not verified: everything on a phone. In particular whether a real finger tap is resolved after the pointerdown listener has moved the region, the frame rate of the ribbon (about 100 clipped draws a frame), the long-press link menu on a ribbon link, scroll momentum inside the two scrollers and how it drives the notes, and what TalkBack announces on the cube.
